faqs.q: I found a raccoon in my Hampton attic — can you move it to the woods?
faqs.a: South Carolina law does not work that way. SCDNR states that routine relocation of wildlife is against state law, and an animal captured near a home must be destroyed or, only with a separate department permit, may be relocated. In Hampton we solve it with eviction and exclusion instead: a one-way door lets the raccoon leave the attic on its own, or the animal is removed under SCDNR depredation rules, and then every entry around rail-town center and creek neighborhoods of the county seat housing is sealed in steel. Raccoons are the top rabies carrier in SC Department of Public Health testing, so droppings and latrine areas are cleaned and sanitized as part of the job.

faqs.q: I saw a snake near my Hampton home. Should I be worried?
faqs.a: Start with identification, not panic. Around Hampton, the everyday snakes are non-venomous rat snakes and racers; the caution species are the copperhead, which is statewide, and the cottonmouth around wet ground, swamp edges, and pond banks. Keep distance, bring pets in, and tell us the size, pattern, and where it sheltered. We identify from photos or on site, handle non-listed snakes where appropriate, and treat venomous encounters as safety work. Reducing cover and rodent food near the foundation lowers repeat sightings more than any single capture. The southern hognose snake of the Sandhills is State Threatened and is referral-only — it is never handled as a removal job.

faqs.q: What does a wildlife removal job in Hampton actually involve?
faqs.a: It starts with the inspection, and the scope grows or shrinks with what that inspection finds around rail-town center and creek neighborhoods of the county seat: how many entry points the animal has opened, whether young are present, and how much exclusion the roofline and crawlspace need. A single squirrel entry sealed in a day is a small job; a raccoon family with latrine cleanup and a full roofline seal is a larger one. We walk you through each item we find before the work is set, so the scope you approve is the scope we do.

Hampton.wildlife_intro:
In Hampton, most of our work starts around the rail-town center and creek neighborhoods of the county seat. More than anything else, we are called for raccoons in pine-edge attics and gray squirrels moving along fence lines.

Older farmhouses on pier foundations, small-town brick homes from the early 1900s, and scattered mobile homes on sandy lots make up most of the housing, with outbuildings on nearly every property. Between the pine stands and the creek bottoms, animals commute along fence rows and field drains, and sandy soil means a burrow opened one week is occupied again the next unless it is screened shut.

The last step on a Hampton call is a walk-around with the homeowner: each entry we sealed, each burrow we screened, and what to watch for when the seasons turn.

Estill.wildlife_intro:
Estill keeps our crew busy around the US 321 farm corridor and swamp country south of Hampton. Two problems account for most visits: armadillos tearing up sandy lawns, and skunks denning beneath outbuildings.

Mill and farm housing from the early twentieth century stands alongside postwar ranches, most of it on crawlspaces that sit low over deep sand. Removal without repair does not hold in Estill, so our visits pair the animal work with sealing and screening sized to the house itself.

faqs.q: Are armadillos really established around Varnville?
faqs.a: Yes. Nine-banded armadillos are established throughout the entirety of South Carolina, and around here they burrow under porches, driveways, and crawlspace edges and root up lawns hunting grubs and worms. We trap the animals working your property and backfill and screen the burrow openings, because an open burrow in this soil is quickly claimed by the next armadillo — or by a skunk or opossum.

faqs.q: We have rats in our Brunson attic. How is that different from squirrels?
faqs.a: Rats work at night and squirrels work at dawn, which is the first clue. In Brunson, roof rats climb from trees, vines, and utility lines around farm and timber roads north of Hampton, while Norway rats burrow along foundations and come up through plumbing gaps. We identify the species, trap inside the structure, and seal the entry points at roof and foundation level — poison alone leaves dead rats in walls and does nothing about the openings.

faqs.q: There are bats in my Brunson attic. When can they be removed?
faqs.a: Bats are excluded, never trapped or killed, and South Carolina requires no permit to remove them. Timing follows SCDNR guidance rather than a state ban: complete exclusions are scheduled for early spring (March–April) or late summer into fall (August–October), because excluding in May through mid-July can trap flightless pups inside. In Brunson we fit one-way exits over the entry points used by colonies near farm and timber roads north of Hampton, seal every other gap of 3/8 inch or more, and clean guano once the colony is out. A single bat found in living quarters is different — do not handle it, and it should go to the SC Department of Public Health for rabies testing.

faqs.q: What will the crew need to do at my Brunson house?
faqs.a: Plan on an inspection first: roofline, attic or crawlspace, and the ground line around the house. From there a Brunson job usually combines removing the animal — by one-way eviction or trapping under depredation rules — with sealing, screening, and any cleanup the animal left behind. Jobs near farm and timber roads north of Hampton with older construction tend to need more sealing; newer homes often need less. The inspection report is what sets the scope, not a phone guess.

faqs.q: When can bats be removed from a Furman home?

What controls the timing is SCDNR guidance, which we follow: complete exclusions are planned for early spring (March-April) or fall (August-October), and we do not run a full exclusion from May through mid-July, sometimes into August, because flightless pups would be trapped inside. That window is agency guidance, not a state law. We can inspect and map every entry at any time of year, and a bat found inside your living space is different — keep the room closed and call us, because bats in living quarters are a rabies-testing situation handled with the Department of Public Health.
